title: Church hurt
hookLine: many have been wounded by Christians; healing may take time and distance

lines: WOUNDED WHERE IT SHOULD BE SAFE.
cards: A woman drives past the church she grew up in. Same red door. Same sign out front with the sermon title in plastic letters.
She hasn't been inside for years, and her stomach still tightens at the sight of it. Somebody in there once told her something about herself, and about God, that she's still trying to unhear.
Friends ask when she'll go back, as if it were a cold she ought to be over. Some people carry wounds that came from Christians, in a place that was meant to be safe.

teach.b: Year one met this with a bruised reed; today goes further. Ezekiel has a whole chapter on it.

God speaks against the shepherds of Israel, the leaders meant to care for the people, and the charges are specific: "The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken."
Then the verdict: "with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them." The text doesn't scold the sheep for scattering.

teach.h: BRING AGAIN WHAT WAS DRIVEN AWAY.
teach.b: God says what he will do himself: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." Some sheep didn't wander off. They were pushed.

teach.h: A BRUISED REED SHALL HE NOT BREAK.
teach.b: Matthew borrows Isaiah's words to describe Jesus: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench." A reed already bent, a lamp wick barely smoking: care that goes slowly with damaged things.

And the Teacher in Ecclesiastes, listing the seasons of a life, includes "a time to heal." Healing has its own season, and it isn't rushed. For some people healing means going back to church, sometimes a different one.
For some it means a long season away. Some never go back.

Some readers draw a gentle way of standing beside a hurt person from these texts: no rushing, no arguing them back, no turning their pain into a debate about defending the institution. Bind up, and let them set the pace.

how: Some Christians who have been hurt in church step away for a season, find a different congregation, or work through it with a counselor or a trusted pastor; some churches run listening sessions or support for people who were harmed.

s: the Bible never criticizes religious leaders who hurt people
Ezekiel 34 charges the shepherds: with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
in Ezekiel, some sheep were driven away, not only lost
God says he will bring again that which was driven away.
Matthew uses the bruised reed to describe Jesus

games.q: in Ezekiel 34, the sheep are scattered, some of them driven away by their own shepherds. what does God say he will do?
o: blame the sheep for wandering off.
seek them, bring them back, and bind up the broken.
leave them to find their own way home.
games.why: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." the anger falls on the shepherds, not the sheep.

practice: Suppose a friend sits down across from you and says, a church hurt me, and notice the first thing you want to say: an explanation, a defense.
Set it down like a heavy bag, and just listen; if the friend is you, listen to yourself the same way, and if you pray, ask that they be bound up gently, at their own pace.
If the hurt included abuse, or ever feels too heavy, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Church hurt. Wounds that come from a church or from Christians. In Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep that were driven away.

orig.note: Hebrew: to heal — from "a time to heal" in Ecclesiastes 3:3.
